paras: The Union Station mob threat against Gordon Donaldson took place on Sunday afternoon, 2 August 1903, when a crowd at Union Station in Indianapolis shouted "lynch him" at Donaldson, a Black special officer of the C., H. & D. Railroad. Police arrested him before he was harmed, and four days later a Police Court judge dismissed the charges against him.

Donaldson had worked as a special officer or watchman in the railroad's yards, and that day an official summoned him to Union Station to give him his discharge. The station was crowded with excursionists.

According to the Indianapolis Journal, Donaldson ordered the crowd to move on and shoved his way to the door, pushing aside a woman holding a baby so that she fell into a man's arms. Shouts of "lynch him" then came "from all sides," and the crowd became what the paper called "a howling mob." Cornered against the wall, Donaldson drew a revolver and said he would kill the first man who touched him. Patrolmen Dolby and Hite then arrived, and he went with them to the police station without resisting.

Railroad officials said Donaldson had no authority at the station, and police said he had used his star to "browbeat" people. On 6 August Judge Whallon of the city Police Court dismissed the case, finding the evidence insufficient on charges of drawing deadly weapons and profanity.

The only coverage found, in the white or the Black press, was in the Indianapolis Journal, and its two reports differed in tone. The first, headlined "NEGRO STARTED TROUBLE," called Donaldson an "impudent negro" with "vicious eyes" and blamed the threats on his "insolence." The follow-up, "Charges Against Colored Officer Arrested Sunday Not Sustained," called his pursuers "a crowd of angry whites" and treated the push only as something they "claimed."

The first report stated as fact that Donaldson threw the woman down, while the later one attributed the charge to the crowd after the court found the evidence insufficient. The first report named only a weapons charge; the second said he was arrested for inciting a riot.

reader.title: Union Station mob threat against Gordon Donaldson
bases: A crowd at the station shouted "lynch him" and turned into a "howling mob" that menaced Donaldson's life until police arrested him, so this was a threatened lynching with no injury reported (A1, A2).
No one was killed: Donaldson went with police unharmed after a crowd threatened to lynch him over the alleged push and his "insolence" (A1, A2). The episode is a threatened lynching, not a lynching.
Both reports come from one paper, the Indianapolis Journal (A1, A2); no other white or Black paper was found.

accounts.label: Indianapolis Journal first report
accounts.gist: Donaldson took an 'authoritative air', shoved people and threw a woman with a baby to the ground; the crowd turned into a howling mob that threatened to lynch him, and he drew a revolver until police arrived.

accounts.label: Railroad officials and police
accounts.gist: Officials said he had no business or authority at the station beyond collecting his discharge; police said he wanted to make a scene and used his star to browbeat people.

accounts.label: Police Court result
accounts.gist: The crowd 'claimed' he knocked down the woman; the judge found the evidence insufficient on the weapons and profanity charges and dismissed the case.

framing.detail: The first report, headlined 'NEGRO STARTED TROUBLE', blamed Donaldson's 'insolence', called him an 'impudent negro' and treated the push as fact, while crediting police with sparing him from violence.
The follow-up, 'Charges Against Colored Officer Arrested Sunday Not Sustained', reported the push only as the crowd's claim and reported the dismissal.

versions.value: He pushed a woman holding a baby with such force that she was thrown to the ground (stated as fact)
The crowd 'claimed' he knocked down a white woman; the court found the evidence insufficient

conflicts.note: A2 is later and reports the court's finding; it treats the push as an unproven claim.

versions.value: Arrested for inciting a riot; charged with drawing deadly weapons and profanity

conflicts.note: Both are from the same paper; A2 adds the riot and profanity charges.

record_check.dossier: A crowd of white travelers and spectators at Union Station, unnamed

record_check.record: accused of pushing a woman carrying a baby to the floor and drawing a revolver
record_check.dossier: Accused of pushing a woman with a baby; he drew the revolver only after the crowd threatened to lynch him, so the revolver belongs to the episode, not to the accusation that set off the crowd

record_check.record: states as fact that Donaldson 'had pushed a woman with a baby'; ends at arrest
record_check.dossier: The push was an accusation the crowd 'claimed'; Judge Whallon dismissed the charges on 6 August for lack of evidence

info: Sunday afternoon, 2 August 1903 ('yesterday afternoon' in the 3 August paper; 'last Sunday' in the 7 August paper)
Union Station, Indianapolis, which was crowded with excursionists
Gordon Donaldson, a "colored" special officer (watchman) of the C., H. & D. Railroad, who had come to the station to receive his discharge
Accused of shoving people and pushing a woman holding a baby so that she fell (A1 states it as fact; A2 says the crowd 'claimed' he knocked down a white woman)
A crowd of travelers and spectators at the station, described as 'angry whites'
Judge Whallon of the Police Court dismissed the case; the evidence was not sufficient to convict on either charge

sources.note: First and fullest report: crowd at Union Station shouted "lynch him" at Donaldson, a colored C., H. & D. special officer accused of pushing a woman with a baby; he drew a revolver; patrolmen arrested him.
quotes: threats of "lynch him" were heard from all sides
The crowd within two minutes changed into a howling mob and vengeance was demanded by the spectators of the negro's insolence.
it is probable that he would have suffered violence at the hands of the infuriated persons who crowded around him and menaced his life

set_aside: A Gordon Donaldson of 383 W. 11th Street inherits money from an uncle; no mention of the station episode, and identity with the officer is not shown.
